title: Some Speculation About Artificial Intelligence and Legal Reasoning
author: Bruce G. Buchanan · Thomas E. Headrick

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Expert systems: Retrieval differs from replacing judgment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between established legal retrieval and proposed systems that answer questions or perform broader legal research. It also reinforces the cluster’s emphasis on knowledge preparation, indexing and cost constraints, while offering proposals rather than evidence that software can replace contextual legal judgment.
qs: At minimum, the computer should be able to retrieve statutes, case language, case summaries, and other legal data, to answer questions about that in- formation, and to communicate in a natural (not cryptic) manner with lawyers.
The ingenuity in designing such a system lies in formu- lating the index, which provides the means of retrieving the legal material.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports selective, human-led deployment: it treats computational capability as restricted to parts of legal problem-solving, identifies semantic and representational barriers, preserves lawyer-client judgment for unclear trade-offs, and declines to forecast wholesale replacement or other social outcomes. It is primarily an exploratory conceptual precursor rather than evidence about modern productivity, verification or operating-model redesign.
qs: 1 Thus, for the more routine language skills that the research system demands, computer capability has been demonstrated, at least for restricted problems.
The lawyer and the client must combine judg- ment as well as they can.

kp.k: Legal AI warrants research, not confident predictions
kp.d: Buchanan and Headrick advocate serious interdisciplinary research into computer simulation of legal reasoning. Writing in 1970, they ground this recommendation in analogous nonlegal programs rather than demonstrated legal reasoning systems, and explicitly decline to assert that computers will or should become legal reasoning aids.
qs: It is premature to state categorically that computers will be used as aids in the process of legal reasoning, or even that they should be.
On this evidence, we have claimed that it would be worthwhile to explore the potential ap- plication of computers to legal reasoning.

kp.k: Legal research constructs arguments rather than retrieves correct answers
kp.d: The authors criticize mutual misconceptions between lawyers and computer scientists: lawyers underestimate computers as mere repositories, while computer scientists mistakenly treat law as facts and correct principles. Their alternative frames legal research as constructing acceptable arguments in pursuit of objectives, not simply locating answers.
qs: But the lawyer rarely looks for, or even expects, clear answers.
More often than not, he searches his data base-treatises, ar- ticles, statutes, cases, and other materials-in order to construct legally acceptable arguments in the pursuit of one or more objectives.

kp.k: Retrieval improves discovery but leaves substantive processing untouched
kp.d: The article surveys keyword and association-factor retrieval systems, identifying the University of Pittsburgh-Aspen System as the only commercially operational system discussed. Such systems can broaden discovery and prioritize reading, but leave lawyers to interpret material and construct arguments. The authors also criticize their neglect of contextual filters such as jurisdiction, procedural posture, facts, and treatment of precedents.
qs: These processes aid a researcher in finding all the documents thar might have some conceivable relationship to the problem under search.
These systems, however, do not aid the researcher in the more important task of processing the output to achieve his desired objective.

kp.k: Semantic processing faces major domain and language constraints
kp.d: The proposed routine research assistant would retrieve legal materials, answer questions, and communicate naturally. The authors report contemporary language capabilities only for restricted problems and emphasize the formidable difficulty of extending them to law's broad subject matter. More sophisticated retrieval would require semantic processing to distinguish meanings rather than merely match words.
qs: Some under- standing of the meaning of sentences, that is, some knowledge of seman- tics, is necessary to avoid such blunders and to provide more help to the lawyer.
Thus, for the more routine language skills that the research system demands, computer capability has been demonstrated, at least for restricted problems.
The practical problems of applying these pioneering programs to as large and complex an area as legal research are formidable indeed.

kp.k: Automation requires articulating and representing lawyers' tacit methods
kp.d: The authors identify eliciting lawyers' decision rules and translating them into usable computational representations as central obstacles. This work may expose weak rational grounds for established judgments and require repeated reformulation, because an initially workable representation need not be the best one. They nevertheless expect the exercise to improve understanding of legal thought independently of any resulting software.
qs: But demands for an intelligent computer system to aid law- yers cannot be met unless lawyers themselves are able to articulate their methods and thought processes.
The problem lies in representing the rules so that the computer can use them.
It may even point out the lack of sub- stantial rational grounds for many decision rules.

kp.k: Two legal reasoning models remain introspective and incomplete
kp.d: The article proposes retrospective argument construction for events that have already occurred and prospective advice about actions clients can still shape. These are conceptual models derived from introspection and discussion with colleagues, not empirical findings about lawyers' work. Both assume that the lawyer has already identified the relevant area of law, leaving initial problem identification outside their main scope.
qs: We have no solid base of data on the legal research process, and, of course, have not attempted an exhaustive description of legal thought processes.
The two models discussed here have been derived from introspection and tested upon our colleagues.

kp.k: Argument construction iterates between facts, rules, and objectives
kp.d: Using Boston Ice Co. v. Potter as an illustration, the authors describe lawyers seeking rules that support a client's desired result, testing factual fit, distinguishing adverse authorities, and revisiting facts as arguments develop. They argue that this task needs a solid sample revealing reasoning in analogous cases rather than every potentially relevant case.
qs: His research strategy is to identify the string of rules that both leads to a desired result and plausibly encompasses a set of facts that accounts for what has happened to his client.
For these processes the lawyer does not need all possibly relevant cases; he needs only a solid sample that indicates how previous courts have usually reasoned and ruled in analogous situations.

kp.k: Prospective advice balances legal risks against business objectives
kp.d: In the second model, lawyers can recommend actions that alter future facts and improve the client's legal position. The Boston Ice example contrasts obtaining express contracts with less formal notification: greater legal security can bring commercial disadvantages. The authors present advice as comparative risk assessment requiring joint lawyer-client judgment rather than mechanical selection of the legally safest option.
qs: Our lawyer might make other suggestions, each entailing some measure of legal risk, which must be balanced against business risks.
The trade-offs may not be clear. The lawyer and the client must combine judg- ment as well as they can.

kp.k: Scientific problem-solving programs offer tentative legal analogies
kp.d: The authors use Heuristic DENDRAL's chemical inference process as their main cross-domain example: analyze data, generate plausible molecular hypotheses, and test candidates while narrowing the search space. They also discuss the General Problem Solver and an investment portfolio program as analogies for goal-directed argument construction and prospective advice. These are demonstrations in other domains, not evidence of successful legal automation.
qs: Although there are many variations on this generate-and-test strat- egy, its fruitfulness for other artificial intelligence programs suggests that it may be a useful approach to legal applications.

Admittedly, it requires a substantial jump to convert Heuristic DEN- DRAL, the simulation of the investment trust officer, or the General Prob- lem Solver into a program that can handle even some of the complexity of law.

kp.k: Fact recognition remains an unresolved legal computing problem
kp.d: The article distinguishes filtering scientific data from recognizing and reinterpreting factual statements in law. DENDRAL and concept-formation programs suggest possible mechanisms for identifying relevant facts and shared characteristics, but the authors report no existing demonstration of the required legal capability. They also note the danger that aggressive filtering can exclude information needed for the best solution.
qs: No existing program shows that computers can successfully recog- nize and reinterpret factual statements, the second of four legal problem- solving processes that a sophisticated legal program should have, but one is at least conceivable.
Computer work has been started; much more remains to be done.

kp.k: Rule conflict methods have uncertain applicability to law
kp.d: The authors explain that heuristic rules may conflict or lack logical completeness. Programs handle this through rule priority, parallel exploration of consequences, additional evidence, or learning to modify rules. A draw-poker learning program illustrates exceptions and generalization, but the authors explicitly leave its applicability to complex legal conflicts unresolved.
qs: Heuristic programs must have some mechanism for handling conflicting decisions, because many if not all of the judg- mental rules are neither logically complete nor internally consistent.
Whether these methods apply in complex legal situations is an open question.

kp.k: Legal analogy exceeds predefined computational relations
kp.d: Geometric analogy programs provide a limited demonstration of analogical reasoning. The authors distinguish using supplied analogies from discovering new ones and argue that legal reasoning would suffer if confined to prespecified dimensions. Even mundane programmed relations might improve performance, but the most inventive legal analogies could remain outside the system's representation.
qs: Discovering analogies in any field is a much harder problem than merely using them.
A legal reasoning program constrained to analogies along similar pre- specified dimensions would be excessively artificial.
Many of the brilliant legal analogies between factual situations or principles are based on rela- tions one probably would not have thought to put into a computer system.

kp.k: Automation could expand access or entrench unequal provision
kp.d: The conclusion offers competing possibilities rather than forecasts: automating laborious work might broaden access to quality service, and widely available usable information might enable self-representation. Conversely, high costs might restrict the system to wealthy users. The article supplies no adoption timetable, cost estimate, or measured access effect.
qs: By removing the "dog work" that underlies quality legal service, the computer system might make good service available to a larger segment of society.
Legal representation might no longer be needed in many disputes.
Because of its cost the system might only be available to the wealthy and would assist them in increasing their wealth.

kp.k: Overreliance and displaced apprenticeship could undermine professional competence
kp.d: The authors speculate that narrow systems might miss possibilities ordinary lawyers recognize and that excessive reliance could lower service quality. Replacing apprentices' work could also disrupt the experiential formation of seasoned judgment. These are expressly hypothetical risks, not observed workforce or training outcomes.
qs: Lawyers might rely too heavily on a restricted, and thus somewhat incompetent, system with a resulting decline in the quality of legal services.

The system might make it difficult to train lawyers for complex tasks requiring seasoned judgment developed through years of apprenticeship, because the apprentice's work had been replaced by ma- chines.

kp.k: Shared systems could reshape legal development and institutional power
kp.d: The authors speculate that common systems used by courts and lawyers might stabilize law but also hinder its adaptation. Computerization could encourage demands for unambiguous, logically complete rules, while control over programming could become a locus of political power. They explicitly caution against choosing among these possible futures on the evidence then available.
qs: With courts and lawyers all using the same system, new stability in the law might be realized.
Control of the system and its programs might confer such significant power that battles over legislation would shift from the committees and floors of legislatures to the offices of programmers.
The selection of any of these outcomes at this point can only be based on prejudice, hope, fear, and the like.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Buchanan and Headrick propose AI research as a way to understand legal reasoning and potentially perform parts of lawyers' work, extending beyond document retrieval.
pts.d: The authors distinguish existing retrieval systems from prospective systems that interpret material, construct arguments and support advice. They envisage goal-directed programs linking facts, rules and desired consequences, and programs suggesting actions that advance clients' goals while limiting adverse legal consequences. These are proposed capabilities, not demonstrated legal applications. They also predict that modelling lawyers' reasoning could improve understanding of legal problem-solving and possibly lawyers' skills.

pts.k: The authors outline possible expansion of access to legal help and, alternatively, substantial substitution for lawyers.
pts.d: Their concluding scenarios include automation of routine work making quality service more widely available, accessible systems enabling self-representation, and reduced need for legal representation or lawyers. They explicitly present these as possible outcomes rather than forecasts they endorse.

pts.k: The authors identify possible degradation of service quality and disruption of apprenticeship.
pts.d: A narrowly capable system might overlook possibilities apparent to ordinary lawyers. Excessive reliance could then reduce service quality. Separately, replacing apprentices' work could make it harder to develop the seasoned judgment needed for complex tasks. The authors also suggest that better understanding of advocated positions could change lawyers' conception of their role.

pts.k: Shared legal systems could change legal stability, institutional power and the distribution of legal-service benefits.
pts.d: The authors speculate that common systems used by courts and lawyers might stabilize law, with either beneficial or harmful consequences for legal development. Pressure to accommodate computers might encourage removal of legal ambiguity. Control of programs could become a locus of political power. Economic possibilities range from prohibitive costs and exclusive access for wealthy users to indispensable savings in legal labour.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The case for research rests on existing nonlegal AI programs and introspective models of legal work, not demonstrated legal-reasoning performance or measured market effects.
pts.d: Buchanan and Headrick survey retrieval systems and restricted natural-language programs, then draw analogies from Heuristic DENDRAL in chemistry, the General Problem Solver, investment-portfolio selection, concept formation, poker learning and geometric analogy. These supply examples of component processes that might transfer to law. Their two models of legal work were derived from introspection and discussion with colleagues. Boston Ice Co. v. Potter illustrates argument construction and prospective advice; it is not a test of an AI system. The authors offer no quantitative legal performance results or empirical evidence for their concluding access, displacement, training, institutional or economic scenarios.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Writing in 1970, the authors advocate immediate research but set no deadline for useful deployment or societal effects.
pts.d: The source consistently conditions future capabilities on successful interdisciplinary research. Lawyers must help articulate their methods; researchers must solve problems of representation, semantics, factual interpretation, rule conflict and analogy. The proposed legal models assume that the problem's legal area has already been identified. Existing programs operate in restricted domains, and extending them to law entails major difficulties. The authors allow outcomes ranging from nonuse or academic confinement to widespread influence, and expressly decline to predict either adoption or desirability.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The scenarios concern practising lawyers, apprentices, clients, ordinary people, courts, researchers and those controlling or financing systems.
pts.d: Practising lawyers might gain research and reasoning assistance, alter their professional roles or face reduced demand. Apprentices might lose work through which judgment develops. Clients might receive better or worse service depending on capability and reliance. Ordinary people might obtain help previously unavailable or represent themselves, while high costs could reserve benefits for wealthy users. Courts and lawyers sharing systems might reshape legal development; programmers and system controllers might acquire power. Lawyers and computer scientists could gain knowledge through research even without practical deployment. The source does not distinguish effects by law-firm size or specific provider-market segment.
